extracted.subtask_description: Guidance on applying the 35 U.S.C. 112, first paragraph written description requirement and related new-matter rules during patent examination, including when and how to make rejections/objections and how to evaluate amendments, genus/species, ranges, priority claims, and incorporation by reference.

rubrics_metrics.name: Amendment affecting a claim
rubrics_metrics.description: An amendment to the claims or the addition of a new claim must be supported by the description of the invention in the application as filed. An amendment to the specification (e.g., a change in the definition of a term used both in the specification and claim) may indirectly affect a claim even though no actual amendment is made to the claim.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cite In re Wright, 866 F.2d 422. When claim language is altered or claims are added, ensure each claim limitation is expressly, implicitly, or inherently supported in the originally filed disclosure. Be mindful that specification amendments can alter claim meaning and thereby raise written description issues.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reliance on filing date of parent application under 35 U.S.C. 120
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims in a U.S. application are entitled to the benefit of an earlier filed U.S. application's filing date only if the subject matter of the claim is disclosed in the manner provided by 35 U.S.C. 112, first paragraph, in the earlier filed application.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate whether the earlier-filed application discloses the claimed subject matter as required by 35 U.S.C. 112, first paragraph. See Tronzo v. Biomet, In re Scheiber.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reliance on priority under 35 U.S.C. 119
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims in a U.S. application are entitled to the benefit of a foreign priority date or provisional application filing date only if the corresponding priority/provisional application supports the claims in the manner required by 35 U.S.C. 112, first paragraph.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess written description support in the priority document itself (35 U.S.C. 119(a)/(e)). See In re Ziegler, Kawai v. Metlesics, In re Gosteli.

rubrics_metrics.name: Support for a claim corresponding to a count in an interference
rubrics_metrics.description: In an interference proceeding, the claim corresponding to a count must be supported by the specification in the manner provided by 35 U.S.C. 112, first paragraph.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A broad generic disclosure to a class of compounds is not necessarily a sufficient written description of a specific compound within the class (Fields v. Conover). When seeking benefit of an earlier-filed U.S. application in an interference, the earlier application must meet 35 U.S.C. 112, first paragraph for the subject matter of the count (Hyatt v. Boone).

rubrics_metrics.name: Presumption of adequate written description and examiner burden
rubrics_metrics.description: A description as filed is presumed to be adequate unless or until sufficient evidence or reasoning to the contrary has been presented by the examiner. The examiner must have a reasonable basis to challenge adequacy and bears the initial burden of presenting by a preponderance of evidence why a person skilled in the art would not recognize in the disclosure a description of the claimed invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cite In re Wertheim and In re Marzocchi. Do not make bare assertions; provide factual reasoning/evidence to rebut the presumption of adequacy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Statement of rejection requirements (written description)
rubrics_metrics.description: When rejecting a claim for lack of written description, the examiner must set forth express findings of fact which support the conclusion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Findings should (A) identify the claim limitation(s) at issue; and (B) establish a prima facie case by providing reasons why a person skilled in the art at the time of filing would not have recognized that the inventor was in possession of the invention as claimed in view of the disclosure. A general allegation of 'unpredictability in the art' is not sufficient. A simple statement pointing out where support is not apparent may suffice for new or amended claims where support is not obvious. When appropriate, suggest claim amendments that can be supported, mindful of the prohibition against adding new matter. See MPEP § 2163.04 and Hyatt v. Dudas.

rubrics_metrics.name: Response to applicant's reply for written description rejections
rubrics_metrics.description: Upon applicant's reply, before repeating any rejection under 35 U.S.C. 112, para. 1 for lack of written description, the examiner must review the basis for the rejection in view of the whole record, including amendments, arguments, and evidence submitted by applicant.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the record shows the written description requirement is satisfied, do not repeat the rejection. If not satisfied, repeat the rejection, fully respond to applicant's rebuttal arguments, and properly treat further showings submitted in the reply. When maintaining a rejection, thoroughly analyze and discuss any affidavits relevant to written description. See In re Alton.

rubrics_metrics.name: Broadening claim — omission of a limitation
rubrics_metrics.description: Omission of a limitation can raise a written description issue as to whether the inventor had possession of a broader, more generic invention. A claim that omits an element described as essential or critical in the original specification does not comply with the written description requirement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider whether the specification describes the omitted element as essential or critical (e.g., Gentry Gallery). Compare cases where a limitation was not considered essential (In re Peters). If omission renders the claim broader than what the disclosure supports, rejection may be appropriate; such claims may also raise enablement or indefiniteness issues under 35 U.S.C. 112 para. 1 or para. 2. See related MPEP § 2172.01.

rubrics_metrics.name: Addition of a generic claim (genus/species support)
rubrics_metrics.description: A claimed genus may be supported by a sufficient description of a representative number of species; one species may suffice only when the disclosure indicates the patentee has invented species sufficient to constitute the genus or where the species is representative and would lead skilled artisans to the genus.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess variation within the genus and whether a sufficient variety of species are described to reflect that variation. A single species is inadequate when ordinary artisans could not predict operability of other species. Conversely, in some situations (e.g., In re Rasmussen, In re Herschler, In re Smythe) disclosure of one species or functional recitation may sufficiently support a genus. Use case law (Enzo Biochem, In re Curtis, Tronzo v. Biomet, In re Gosteli) to guide the analysis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Narrowing or subgeneric claim
rubrics_metrics.description: Introducing claim changes that narrow claims by adding elements or limitations not supported by the as-filed disclosure violates the written description requirement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A 'laundry list' of possibilities does not constitute written description of every species (Fujikawa v. Wattanasin). It may be improper to claim a subgenus that was not reasonably communicated by the original disclosure (In re Lukach). Each case depends on whether the original disclosure would reasonably convey the subgenus to those skilled in the art (In re Wilder).

rubrics_metrics.name: Range limitations
rubrics_metrics.description: When changing numerical range limitations, the analysis must consider which ranges one skilled in the art would consider inherently supported by the original disclosure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: original ranges of 25%-60% with specific examples of 36% and 50% did not support a new claim to 'at least 35%' because it read on embodiments outside the disclosed 25%-60% range, but 'between 35% and 60%' did meet the requirement (In re Wertheim). Consider whether the specification clearly discloses that a claimant considered a numeric ratio to be part of the invention (Purdue Pharma v. Faulding) and whether combinations of ranges are adequately described (Union Oil v. Atlantic Richfield).

rubrics_metrics.name: Relationship of written description requirement to new matter (statutory prohibitions)
rubrics_metrics.description: If an applicant amends or attempts to amend the abstract, specification or drawings to add content not described in the application as filed, an issue of new matter arises. Two statutory provisions prohibit introduction of new matter: 35 U.S.C. 132 (No amendment shall introduce new matter) and 35 U.S.C. 251 (No new matter in reissue).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat added subject matter in any part of the application consistently: information in specification, claims, or drawings as filed can be added to other parts without introducing new matter, but adding new content where none existed is prohibited. See MPEP § 2163.06.

rubrics_metrics.name: Treatment of new matter (examiners' actions)
rubrics_metrics.description: If new subject matter is added to the disclosure, the examiner should object to the introduction of new matter under 35 U.S.C. 132 or 251 as appropriate, and require applicant to cancel the new matter. If new matter is added to the claims, the examiner should reject the claims under 35 U.S.C. 112, first paragraph - written description requirement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Even if claims are not directly amended, an amendment to the specification that adds material affecting claim limitations should trigger a 112, first paragraph rejection. The examiner should still consider added claim matter in prior art rejections because a new matter rejection may be overcome by the applicant.

rubrics_metrics.name: Review of new matter objections and/or rejections
rubrics_metrics.description: Rejection of claims is reviewable by the Board of Patent Appeals and Interferences; an objection and requirement to delete new matter is subject to supervisory review by petition under 37 CFR 1.181.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If both rejection and objection are made (claims and specification contain new matter), the issue becomes appealable and should not be decided by petition. Follow appropriate appeal/petition routes described.

rubrics_metrics.name: Claimed subject matter not disclosed in remainder of specification
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims as filed are part of the disclosure; if an application as originally filed contains a claim disclosing material not disclosed in the remainder of the specification, the applicant may amend the specification to include the claimed subject matter.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use Form Paragraph 7.44 where originally claimed subject matter lacks proper antecedent basis in the specification. See In re Benno.

rubrics_metrics.name: Amendments supported in the original description — rephrasing permitted
rubrics_metrics.description: Amendments to an application which are supported in the original description are NOT new matter. Mere rephrasing of a passage that preserves the same meaning is permissible. Inclusion of dictionary or art-recognized definitions known at the time of filing is not new matter.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cite In re Anderson. If multiple definitions exist for a term and a definition is added, there must be clear indication from the application as filed that applicant intended that particular definition (Scarring Corp. v. Megan). Substituting a more specific name for a previously used generic term may be permissible if it merely 'renames' the invention and is supported by original deposits or disclosure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Obvious errors correction
rubrics_metrics.description: An amendment to correct an obvious error does not constitute new matter where one skilled in the art would both recognize the existence of an error in the specification and the appropriate correction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cite In re Odd. Do not rely on foreign priority documents of record to support correction of an error in the pending U.S. application (Ex parte Bondiou), unless the U.S. application explicitly incorporates the foreign priority document by reference. For applications filed on or after Sept. 21, 2004, inadvertent omission of portions may be addressed under 37 CFR 1.55 with conditions of 37 CFR 1.57(a) and MPEP § 201.17.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inherent function, theory, or advantage may be later recited
rubrics_metrics.description: By disclosing a device that inherently performs a function or has a property, operates according to a theory or has an advantage, an application necessarily discloses that function/theory/advantage even if not explicitly stated; the application may later be amended to recite it without introducing new matter.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cite In re Reynolds and In re Smythe. To establish inherency via extrinsic evidence, the evidence 'must make clear that the missing descriptive matter is necessarily present... and that it would be so recognized by persons of ordinary skill.' Inherency cannot be established by probabilities or possibilities (In re Robertson).

rubrics_metrics.name: Incorporation by reference
rubrics_metrics.description: Information incorporated by reference into the specification is as much a part of the application as if the text were repeated in the application; replacing the identified material incorporated by reference with the actual text is not new matter.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Follow 37 CFR 1.57 and MPEP § 608.01(p) for Office policy regarding incorporation by reference. Treat incorporated material as part of the original disclosure for written description/new matter analysis.
